newsitem.title: USA: Economist Gramlich a pragmatic consensus builder.
newsitem.headline: Economist Gramlich a pragmatic consensus builder.

text.p: Edward Gramlich, a University of Michigan professor who is emerging as a likely nominee to the Federal Reserve Board, is a seasoned economist known for his pragmatism and consensus building.

A U.S. official said on Thursday that Gramlich, dean of the university's School of Public Policy, had surfaced as a candidate likely to be nominated by President Bill Clinton to one of the two vacancies on the central bank's board.

Gramlich's experience includes serving as a Fed researcher in the 1960s, spending nearly 20 years on the University of Michigan faculty as well as a brief stint as deputy and acting director of the Congressional Budget Office in 1986 and 1987.
He has done considerable research on tax and budget policy, social welfare and the economics of major league baseball.

For the past two years, the economist has been best known as chairman of the federal government's Advisory Council on Social Security, which in January issued a report on ways to plug the pension system's future financing gap.

The panel delivered three separate recommendation plans: one maintaining the pay-as-you-go system with minor changes; a second shifting much of the resources and responsibility for retirement investment to individuals; and a third plan -- championed by Gramlich -- that would protect most benefits while allowing some individual control over investments.

"He wants to solve the problems; he's not an idealogue," said Marc Twinney, a retired Ford Motor Co. pension director who served on the council with Gramlich. "I think he's very good with people to understand their positions. He worked hard to get the 13 members to work together to reach one plan."

Gramlich's Social Security plan calls for gradual benefit cuts mainly for higher-wage workers and a slight increase in the retirement age. It would keep the current 12.4 percent payroll tax but would add a 1.6 percentage-point increase that would be diverted to individual investment accounts.
But rather than allowing a huge array of risky investment options, his plan would only allow people to choose among five to 10 broad indexed mutual funds covering stocks and bonds.

"I would preserve the important social protections of Social Security and still achieve long-term financial balance through what might be called kind and gentle benefit cuts," Gramlich wrote in a New York Times article in January. "Most of the cuts would be felt by high-wage workers, with disabled and low-wage workers being largely protected from the cuts."
He also has been critical of groups that do not want to change the current system.
"To say that we don't need to raise taxes and we don't need to cut benefits and we can 'study' equity investments, that's bordering on being irresponsible," he told the Detroit News in January.

A native of Rochester, N.Y., Gramlich received his master's and doctoral degrees from Yale University. He is married with two grown children. He is the author of a popular textbook on cost-benefit analysis, which is now in its second edition.
